lines.text: The king.
The Netherlands is a kingdom [koninkrijk]: no president, but a king.
Willem-Alexander is the current king.
His immediate family is the royal house [koningshuis].
He is married to Queen Máxima; they have three daughters.
The eldest, Princess Amalia, will become queen later.
The king has little power [weinig macht], but he is 'the face' of the Netherlands: he goes on state visits [staatsbezoek].
That is the ceremonial [ceremoniële] function.
Once a year, on Prinsjesdag (the third Tuesday of September), he presents the ministers' plans.
The government [De regering] is the administration of the country: the king [koning], the prime minister [minister-president] and the ministers together.
The prime minister is the leader of the ministers.
Each minister has their own portfolio (for example Education or Finance).
A state secretary [staatssecretaris] (junior minister) supports a minister.
All ministers and state secretaries together are called the cabinet [kabinet].
The parliament.
The Netherlands is a democracy [democratie]: the inhabitants choose the government.
The Tweede Kamer has 150 members, the Eerste Kamer has 75 members.
Together they are the parliament [parlement].
The parliament monitors/oversees [controleert] the government and can pass [aannemen] laws or not.
Laws first go to the Tweede Kamer, then to the Eerste Kamer.
Members of the Tweede Kamer may themselves make proposals [voorstellen] for new laws.
The parliament and the government are located in Den Haag.
Governing the country, the province and the municipality.
All organizations at these levels belong to the authorities/public administration [overheid]:

| Government of | Leader | Parliament |
|---|---|---|
| the Netherlands | the minister-president | Eerste and Tweede Kamer |
| the province | the King's Commissioner [commissaris van de Koning] | the Provinciale Staten |
| the municipality | the mayor [burgemeester] | the municipal council [gemeenteraad] |
The Tweede Kamer decides on matters for the whole country (defense, civic integration, education).
The Provinciale Staten decide on roads, housing and nature areas in the province.
The municipality takes care of, for example, enough social rental housing and help for people.
The three powers.
There are three kinds of power:
Legislative power [Wetgevende macht]: the government and parliament together — they make the laws.
Executive power [Uitvoerende macht]: the government; ministers direct civil servants [ambtenaren] who carry out the laws.
Judicial power [Rechterlijke macht]: the judges [rechters].
These powers operate separately: the separation of powers [scheiding van de machten].
The government may not tell a judge what to decide.
This way no single power can obtain all the power.
The powers also keep each other in check.
Political parties.
Members of the Tweede Kamer and the municipal council belong to a political party [politieke partij].
Within a party, people have roughly the same ideas.
Anyone can become a member [lid].
Types of parties:
Left-wing parties [Linkse partijen]: the gap between rich and poor should be smaller; the rich pay more tax [belasting]; benefits [uitkeringen] must be high enough.
Right-wing parties [Rechtse partijen]: people should take care of themselves as much as possible; good for big companies; the state should not borrow too much.

Progressive parties [Progressieve partijen] think it is good that society [maatschappij] changes; conservative parties [conservatieve partijen] prefer little change (for example regarding abortion or migration).
Left-wing parties are often progressive and right-wing parties conservative.
The voting compass [Kieskompas] shows where the parties stand.
Elections.
Before the elections, parties write election programs [programma's] and advertise.
People vote for a party or a person.
Voting is not compulsory [niet verplicht].
Elections for the Tweede Kamer are held once every four years.
Afterwards, parties form a coalition [coalitie] (usually the largest party with a few others).
The coalition looks for ministers and state secretaries: the new government is made up of the governing parties [regeringspartijen].
If the ministers stop working together, the cabinet has fallen [gevallen]; then there are usually new elections.
Which elections are there?

For: 1) the municipality [gemeente] (gemeenteraad, every 4 years), 2) the province [provincie] (Provinciale Staten, every 4 years — they elect the Eerste Kamer), 3) the water board [waterschap] (responsible for dikes, water levels and clean waste water; drinking water comes from the water company; every 4 years, at the same time as the Provinciale Staten), 4) the country [land] (Tweede Kamer, every 4 years), 5) Europe [Europa] (European Parliament, every 5 years).
The Netherlands has twelve provinces.
Who may vote?
Adults aged 18 and older.
For the gemeenteraad: residents with a passport of the Netherlands or the EU, or residents from outside the EU who have lived in the Netherlands legally for five years or longer.
For the Provinciale Staten and the Tweede Kamer: only people with Dutch nationality [Nederlandse nationaliteit].
For the waterschap: residents, sometimes also without Dutch nationality.
For the European Parliament: residents of the EU with an EU nationality.
Active and passive voting rights.
Active suffrage [Actief kiesrecht]: you may vote yourself.
Passive suffrage [Passief kiesrecht]: other people may vote for you; you are then on a candidate list.
In the Netherlands the rules for both are the same.
A referendum is a separate kind of election: you can only say 'yes' (in favor) or 'no' (against) to a proposal.
